email.body:
The owner suggested sharing a wedding video. It could give couples a glimpse of a wedding there before they came to see the space themselves.

Our team proposed an extra email for those later appointments, using her idea to help couples look forward to the visit and giving them an opening to ask questions.

The opportunity we were discussing was the time before the tour. A couple had expressed enough interest to make an appointment, and there was still room to help them become more familiar with the venue before arriving.

**We believe those weeks deserve a place in the advertising strategy.**

When your marketing already brings in inquiries and tours, that interval is another part of the experience worth considering. The visit itself matters, and so does the opportunity to build interest while a couple waits for it.

That's a conversation I want us to be able to have with venue owners. We can bring an advertising perspective, listen to what the owner knows and develop ideas together, while the venue team continues to lead the personal relationship.

For owners who want that kind of partnership, ELEVATE is our full-service advertising management program. We manage your Google and Meta advertising, with follow-up support alongside it, while your venue team handles the personal conversations and tours.

The way we think about the work should make room for what couples experience after they inquire, including the time before they walk through your doors.

Talk soon,
Whitney

slides.text:
In a conversation with a venue owner, we discussed couples who had appointments further ahead.

The visit was on the calendar, but the couple wouldn't experience the property in person just yet. That gave us a useful question to explore together: what might help the venue feel more familiar and appealing during the wait?

slides.job: Give the owner clear credit for the wedding video idea.
slides.text:
The owner suggested a video showing a wedding at the venue.

Her idea gave the conversation something concrete to work with. Couples could have a way to see the place as a wedding setting before touring it themselves. We could discuss the possibility of building anticipation around the visit, using the idea she brought forward.

slides.job: Show WIA's contribution as a proposal.
slides.text:
Our team proposed an additional email for the couples whose tours were further away.

The message could share the video and welcome questions before the appointment. We were developing the owner's suggestion into a possible point of contact during the waiting period, with the aim of helping couples become more interested in seeing the venue.

slides.job: Connect the scene to an owner whose marketing already works.
slides.text:
When your venue is already attracting inquiries, a scheduled tour is a meaningful next step.

It also creates an interval between a couple choosing to visit and actually arriving. That time deserves consideration within the experience of the people your advertising reaches. The opportunity is to continue giving them reasons to look forward to meeting you.

slides.job: Deepen the reframe without providing account steps.
slides.text:
A future appointment gives you a date. It also gives the couple time.

They may be able to learn more about the venue before standing in it. We believe an advertising discussion can make room for that possibility, alongside attracting the initial inquiry. The waiting period can be considered on its own terms, rather than only as the lead-up to a reminder.

slides.job: State the belief and preserve the venue's sales responsibility.
slides.text:
**We believe advertising strategy should include the experience before a couple visits.**

That means making space to discuss how their interest could be supported after they schedule a tour. It doesn't give the advertising team ownership of the personal relationship. The venue still answers couples, leads the conversations and welcomes them onto the property.

slides.job: Make the value of WIA's thinking explicit.
slides.text:
This is the perspective we want to bring to the table with an owner.

An inquiry tells us someone wants to know more. A later tour gives us an opportunity to discuss what could sustain and develop that interest before the visit. We can contribute to that conversation while keeping the venue's own knowledge and ideas at its centre.

slides.job: Close for both management and guided-support readers without an offer CTA.
slides.text:
Whether you want a team to manage your advertising or to launch your campaigns and guide you while you run them, that broader perspective matters.

We believe the partnership should make room for the time before couples arrive, as well as the work of reaching them. Your venue's waiting period deserves thoughtful attention from the people helping you advertise.

prior_content_context.argument: We treat the weeks before a venue tour as part of the advertising strategy, helping couples stay interested before they can visit.
prior_content_context.audience: Venue owners who already attract inquiries and book tours, and want their advertising team to understand what happens while couples are waiting to visit.
prior_content_context.mechanism: Whitney proposed an earlier phone conversation or personal virtual preview before a later tour. The venue owner suggested a video, and our team developed that into a possible pre-tour follow-up that would build excitement and invite questions.

prior_content_context.argument: We keep upcoming dates in the ad strategy by finding a reason they're right for couples now, including a venue's ability to host a wedding without a long engagement.
prior_content_context.audience: Venue owners already advertising who are planning their next season's calendar and want their ads to reflect what their team can actually offer couples.
prior_content_context.mechanism: Whitney asked what made spring weddings at the venue appealing, then explored seasonal food and drink. She also proposed explaining that couples didn't need a long engagement because the venue had a team that could pull the wedding together.

prior_content_context.argument: When couples book a venue tour well in advance, the business may need to keep the venue in consideration without expanding into tour times that do not fit its staffing or preparation constraints. A personalized preview before the visit is a possible alternative to treating schedule expansion as the only response.
prior_content_context.audience: Wedding-venue owners whose couples book tours more than two weeks ahead and who cannot readily add weekend or early-morning appointments.
prior_content_context.mechanism: The venue owner said couples sometimes found another venue before their scheduled visit, while also describing limits on Saturday tours and drawbacks to Sunday appointments. Whitney proposed a phone or video touchpoint and a supplemental message for people whose tours were booked farther out; these were ideas, not tested interventions.

prior_content_context.argument: We keep the wedding a venue hosts today separate from the one its owner is planning, so the details in its ads match what couples can experience.
prior_content_context.audience: Venue owners refining their spaces or adding wedding packages who want their ads to represent the business accurately as it grows.
prior_content_context.mechanism: When Carli asked whether to describe her hoped-for wedding or what actually happens, Whitney asked for the current couple's experience. Later, Whitney checked whether proposed patio draping was a future improvement.

prior_content_context.argument: We start by understanding how couples already buy from your wedding business, so our advertising recommendations build on the work you've already done.
prior_content_context.audience: Wedding business owners who already run ads and have built useful systems for inquiries, information and booking. They want a dedicated advertising team that understands that work.
prior_content_context.mechanism: Whitney traced the prospect's first inquiry through to an automated information page, checking how calls, texts and emails were answered. After the owner explained that process, Whitney recognised the existing infrastructure before describing WIA's usual inquiry and nurture setup.

prior_content_context.argument: We treat an owner's firsthand knowledge of her weddings as evidence for the ad strategy, even when the search numbers are small.
prior_content_context.audience: Venue owners who already have years of real weddings and strong content behind them, and want an advertising team that understands what those weddings reveal.
prior_content_context.mechanism: Carmen heard Carli describe the dogs already appearing in her venue's Instagram content and chose to include dog-friendly wedding searches in the proposed keyword list. She made that choice even though the search volume she reported was small.

prior_content_context.argument: A wedding venue's ad creative can serve different purposes for people at different stages: introduce the venue to unfamiliar audiences, invite an inquiry or tour when seeking action, and address choice questions for people already familiar with it.
prior_content_context.audience: Wedding venues planning or reviewing paid campaigns for audiences ranging from people who have not encountered the venue to people who have already inquired or scheduled a tour.
prior_content_context.mechanism: The proposed plan distinguishes cold-audience introductions, conversion ads asking for an inquiry or tour, and retargeting that addresses objections and reasons to book. The message changes with the audience's decision stage; the exchange describes an intended approach, not demonstrated campaign results.

prior_content_context.argument: Email opens can show that a message was viewed, but clicks offer a different signal about which content prompted an action. They discussed examining the content of those emails, including a guest-entertainment guide and weather or backup-plan information, as material worth reviewing rather than proof of booking causation.

prior_content_context.argument: A clear self-service path can let suitable prospects check practical fit questions before they need personal attention, while leaving room for the inquiries that require help. The useful design question is what couples can confidently assess on their own and where a human response still matters.
prior_content_context.audience: Wedding-business owners with established inquiry systems who are considering whether to make pricing, availability, location, or next steps easier to assess without a conversation.
prior_content_context.mechanism: An elopement planner described a self-built flow that let prospects view pricing, availability, and locations and follow steps toward a quote. prior_content_context.argument: A wedding photographer's positioning is more useful when it distinguishes candid coverage from staged imagery without implying that couples will be left unguided when they want help.
prior_content_context.audience: Wedding photographers with an established visual style who are refining ad messaging for couples deciding whether the photographer's approach will suit them.
prior_content_context.mechanism: The photographer reported that many couples value real moments and also ask for help with couple portraits. Messaging that reflects both parts can address the style preference without obscuring the practical support those couples may want.

message_spine: Start with the buyer's setting, not the number of places the business serves: ask what the page must help this couple evaluate [C3].
Check meaningful differences in imagery and offer context without assuming geography determines preferences [C3].
Choose an initial scope: retain a coherent shared page or focus on a priority market. Present these as options, not a proven hierarchy [C3].
Consider venue-specific context only as an untested application of the regional principle, without promising a measured improvement [C4].

prior_content_context.argument: When a wedding business serves regions with different visual expectations, a market-specific landing page can make the offer easier to evaluate than asking one page to represent both markets at once.
prior_content_context.audience: Wedding photographers serving more than one region who are deciding how to focus advertising and landing-page content while managing a limited initial scope.
prior_content_context.mechanism: In the reported discussion, the photographer said Colorado couples often want to see mountains while Florida couples often do not, and connected that difference to difficulty targeting both through one landing page. Different visual expectations can change what makes the page feel relevant to a couple evaluating the location.

prior_content_context.argument: A search term that appears stylistically misaligned is not automatically a negative keyword when couples may use style labels imprecisely and some inquiries using the term may still be suitable.
prior_content_context.audience: Wedding photographers managing search campaigns who have a defined visual style and are weighing lead relevance against excluding potentially useful searches.
prior_content_context.mechanism: The photographer reported that some inquiries included the term and that one of roughly four or five people who mentioned it in the last year became a client. That small account does not establish keyword performance, but it illustrates why the search phrase, inquiry context, and eventual fit need to be considered before excluding it.

prior_content_context.argument: When one ad is spending without tracked leads, the useful decision may be to pause that specific campaign while preserving other campaigns with a different temporary purpose. An account-wide stop-or-continue judgment can obscure which activity is actually in question.
prior_content_context.audience: Wedding-business owners reviewing paid campaigns who are concerned about spend but have several ads serving different purposes.
prior_content_context.mechanism: The account review described one Meta lead campaign limited to people who had visited the website in the previous 45 days. prior_content_context.argument: For a small wedding business considering lead-management software, an ongoing subscription can remain the decisive affordability concern even when the setup work seems worth paying for and the system appears useful.
prior_content_context.audience: Owners of small wedding businesses evaluating recurring software or lead-management costs, especially those with limited booking volume or lower-cost tools already in use.
prior_content_context.mechanism: In one sales conversation, a photographer who takes up to about 20 weddings a year distinguished the setup fee from the ongoing cost and compared it with a free tool she was using. prior_content_context.argument: When traffic rises without clearly stronger leads, reducing spend need not mean making the largest possible cut. A more measured reset can preserve room to compare channels and reassess the budget against conversion and lead-quality evidence.
prior_content_context.audience: Wedding-business owners already investing in paid ads who want to reduce spend but do not yet have clear evidence about which channel or lead source is working better.
prior_content_context.mechanism: In this account discussion, the owner reported increased traffic without clearly stronger leads. The team recommended a lower Google Ads budget than the existing spend, an initially fairly even Google and Meta split, and later reallocation based on data. The recommendation connected budget restraint to a plan for comparison rather than an assumption that more traffic meant better leads.
